summary: This article from The Wildest, written by Shauna S. Roberts, PhD and Dr. Alycia Washington, DVM, MS, surveys common eye disorders in dogs and how they are treated. It explains how canine eyes work, which breeds are prone to particular problems, and the warning signs owners should watch for. It stresses early veterinary care, with referral to a veterinary ophthalmologist when needed.
one_line: A guide to common canine eye disorders, their breed risks, warning signs, anatomy, and treatment, with advice to see a vet early.
key_facts: Dogs have only two types of cones, compared with three types in human eyes, so dogs do not see as many colors as people.
The tapetum lucidum is a reflective lining behind the retina that makes dogs' eyes glow and helps them see in dim light.
Dogs' eyes have a third eyelid called the nictitating membrane, a thin whitish-pink tissue that protects the eye.
Cataracts are the most common cause of blindness in dogs, and they are a clouding of the lens.
Glaucoma is elevated pressure created by fluid inside the eyeball draining more slowly than it is produced.
Corneal ulcers are slow-healing sores on the dog's cornea accompanied by inflammation, and most are caused by injuries.
Cherry eye occurs when the third eyelid gland becomes displaced and protrudes, looking like smooth, pink tissue at the inside corner of the eye.
Progressive retinal atrophy (PRA) is a group of retinal disorders in which rods and cones die off, and there is no treatment for it.
Only about 300 veterinarians in the United States have board certification from the American College of Veterinary Ophthalmologists.
Brachycephalic breeds include Pugs, French Bulldogs, English Bulldogs, Boston Terriers, Lhasa Apsos, and Bullmastiffs.
Dr. Samuel J. Vainisi, DVM, ACVO of the Animal Eye Clinic in Denmark, Wisc., says small breeds with very short noses and big eyeballs are more prone to eye injuries.
Never apply human medications to a dog's eyes without first consulting a veterinarian, since human medications may worsen the condition.
Watery eyes, or epiphora, occur either from excess tear production due to irritation or from poor drainage through the nasolacrimal duct.
Dry eye may be treated with artificial tears, good eye hygiene, anti-inflammatory drugs, and/or cyclosporine ointment (Optimmune).
